newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia announces 500 bln peso budget freeze.
newsitem.headline: Colombia announces 500 bln peso budget freeze.

text.p: Colombia's Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo announced a 500 billion peso budget freeze from Monday in a bid to rein in the yawning fiscal deficit.

In an afternoon press conference he said the measures were aimed at cutting the deficit by an estimated 0.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP). The deficit originally forecast this year was 1.1 percent of GDP, compared to a total fiscal deficit in the government and public sector of 1.04 percent of GDP in 1996.
Ocampo denied the budget freeze was linked to the forthcoming visit of International Monetary Fund chief Michel Camdessus, who is due to meet President Ernesto Samper onThursday.

In an IMF report leaked to the Colombian media, Camdessus is understood to be highly critical of Samper's short and medium term policies, which he said were aimed more at creating short term economic growth than building solid foundations for an economy that would be "robust and healthy" in the longer term.

The Finance Minister and the head of the National Planning Department, Cecilia Lopez, said investment budgets would be thoroughly reviewed and in some cases spending originally programmed for this year would be held back until next year.

Both were careful to avoid calling the move a budget cut, saying instead that they were creating a "more sincere" budget. "We are announcing a 500 billion peso budget freeze to take place with immediate effect with the aim of speeding up the reduction in the budget deficit by linking parts of the 1997 and 1998 budgets," Ocampo said.

The Finance Minister and the head of the National Planning Department, Cecilia Lopez, said investment budgets would be thoroughly reviewed and in some cases spending originally programmed for this year would be held back until next year.
Both were careful to avoid calling the move a budget cut, saying instead that they were creating a "more sincere" budget.
He praised the efficiency of road building, potable water programs, health and education but criticized wasteful spending in justice.
Ocampo, however, refrained from criticizing military and police spending, saying he had no effective way of measuring efficiency levels in that sector.

Lopez said all government departments and public sector operations would present reports to the government in the coming weeks through which efficiency levels would be analyzed and revised budget allocations calculated.

In January, the government pushed through a congressional bill to slash 1.3 trillion pesos of the total national budget of about 30 trillion pesos. It proposed additional measures to rein in the yawning fiscal deficit under an economic state of emergency plan, but this was later declared unconstitutional by Colombia's Constituional Court.
